groups.text: A new pod joins under load.
Its main is a few lines, yet it takes a while to answer, then answers slowly for a while.
Where does the time go?
First the launcher loads the J V M library, which creates a VM: it reserves the heap, generates its interpreter, and starts its threads.
Then the classes.
A three hundred-class test app loads one thousand five hundred thirty-seven of them on J D K twenty-one, with class sharing off.
nine hundred eleven come from the J D K, and three hundred twenty-five are hidden classes made for lambdas.
Yours are a fifth.
For each one, the J V M finds the class file, parses it into metaspace, and verifies the bytecode.
It runs the static initializer later, on first use.
Your code starts in the interpreter, one bytecode at a time.
The jit turns hot methods into machine code, but only once it has profiles: counts of what the code really does.
A framework adds its own work: scanning for annotations, wiring beans, generating proxies, parsing config.
Now restart the J V M.
How much of this work does it skip?
Almost none. Nothing survives the process, except a default archive of about one thousand three hundred J D K classes, already parsed.
Those are mapped from disk.
Everything else is done again.
A tiny HTTP server on J D K twenty-one: the VM is ready at thirty milliseconds, the app logs started at one hundred three, and the first two hundred arrives at one hundred seventy-nine.
With the archive off, about two hundred thirty-five to three hundred twenty.
Even then it isn't at full speed.
The fastest code comes only after a method has run often.
You can watch it with -Xlog:class+load.
Each line says where a class came from: the archive, the J D K, your jar, or the class that made it.
The rule: start-up is work the J V M repeats on every launch.
Every class, a cold jit, and the framework's own work.
Quick check. A hidden class has no class file.
Why can its source never start with file?
Because file names the jar a class was read from, and a hidden class never had one.
